title: Global Barter — 100 currencies inspired by the world's barter traditions
status: Design concepts inspired by real barter and exchange traditions. Not legal tender, not for sale, no cash value, no redemption, no investment rights. The traditions belong to the people who keep them; each note cites a source.
art: Each currency carries a different actual numbered Noun, #0 through #99, each used once. Pixels are drawn from the official CC0 Nouns trait data using the on-chain seed retrieved from the Nouns subgraph and recorded in public/images/nouns-money/source-100/provenance.json, where the renders are checked against the official RLE data.

regions.name: Africa & the Middle East
regions.summary: Caravan trades, market days, salt bars and the community-credit networks that keep neighborhoods trading when cash runs short.

regions.name: Europe
regions.summary: From barter rings and business mutual-credit circuits to the old work parties where a village turned out for one farm at a time.

regions.name: Asia
regions.summary: Mountain caravans, river markets, barter fairs and the labor exchanges that bring in a harvest or rethatch a roof.

regions.name: Oceania & the Pacific
regions.summary: Island markets, trading voyages, seasonal gatherings and community swaps across the Pacific, described as the communities themselves describe them.

regions.name: The Americas
regions.summary: Trueque markets, communal work days, trade-post units of account and the barter clubs that carried neighbors through hard years.

regions.name: Global networks
regions.summary: Practices that crossed borders: time banks, home and seed swaps, repair cafés and other networks where people trade help and things directly.

currencies.name: Nnoboa Turn
currencies.line: Neighbours take turns weeding each member's farm.
currencies.how: Turns are earned by working a day on another member's farm and spent when the group comes to yours, especially at weeding time. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Nnoboa is an Akan custom in which neighbours take turns working each member's fields; an IFPRI study dates it to the pre-colonial era, before cocoa cooperatives arrived in the late 1920s.
currencies.source_title: Farmer-Based Organizations in Ghana (IFPRI Ghana Strategy Support Program)
currencies.noun_fit: Southern Ghana is cocoa country, and a chocolatey cookie is the sweetest nod to it.

currencies.name: Debo Day
currencies.line: Neighbours work your field; you feed them and repay the favour.
currencies.how: Days are earned by joining a neighbour's weeding or harvest and spent when your own field needs hands; the host provides the meal. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In debo, Ethiopian farmers call neighbours to work their fields, feed them and later repay the help; in the related wenfel, every member receives the group's labour in turn.
currencies.source_title: Community social labour-share groups (Debo/Wenfel) [Ethiopia] (WOCAT)
currencies.noun_fit: The clover on its chest stands for the fields, and the icepop for the cool-down after a day of weeding.

currencies.name: Silent Shore
currencies.line: Goods left on the sand and answered in kind, with no words spoken.
currencies.how: Beacons are earned by leaving goods on a shared swap shelf that others accept and spent on items left there; nobody has to meet. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Herodotus, writing c. 430 BCE, told of Carthaginians leaving goods on an African shore beyond the Pillars of Heracles and withdrawing while locals set out gold, until both sides were satisfied.
currencies.source_title: Silent trade (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
currencies.noun_fit: A rangefinder is all about judging distance, and in silent trade both sides kept theirs.

currencies.name: Tiwizi Hands
currencies.line: Households pool labour for harvests, houses and shared channels.
currencies.how: Hands are earned by joining a group job, such as a harvest, a roof or a channel clean-up, and spent when your household needs a crew. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Tiwizi, from the Amazigh word for cooperation, is a centuries-old Maghrebi custom of pooling labour for harvests, house-building and shared irrigation; Moroccan groups still organise it.
currencies.source_title: Twiza: Activating a Maghrebian tradition of cooperation and mutual aid (DVV International)
currencies.noun_fit: A shared work day runs until the sun sets over the Atlas, so tiwizi gets the sunset.

currencies.name: Swop Shop
currencies.line: Collected recyclables swapped for groceries and school supplies.
currencies.how: Points are earned by bringing sorted recyclables to a community swap counter and spent on groceries, toiletries or school supplies. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: South African swop shops began in 2003 in Zwelihle, Hermanus, letting residents trade collected recyclables for points spent on everyday goods; Cape Town's mobile Swop Shop relaunched in 2025.
currencies.source_title: City's mobile Swop Shop brings recycling rewards closer to home (City of Cape Town)
currencies.noun_fit: Swop shops turn what would have gone in the bin into groceries, so the trashcan earns its place.

currencies.name: Milk for Grain
currencies.line: Women's milk and butter traded with farming neighbours for grain.
currencies.how: Calabashes are earned by bringing dairy, eggs or garden produce to a neighbourhood swap and spent on grain or other staples. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Fulani women have long processed milk and butter and traded them with farming neighbours for household grain; ODI research documented this dairy trade among settled Fulani in central Nigeria.
currencies.source_title: Dairying by settled Fulani women in central Nigeria (ODI)
currencies.noun_fit: Butter from one side, grain from the other: between them they make buttered toast.

currencies.name: Copper Deben
currencies.line: Prices set in weights of copper, paid in grain, oil or cloth.
currencies.how: Prices are posted in Deben, a fixed reckoning unit, and members settle in goods or help of equal reckoning. Deben are earned by contributing and are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In New Kingdom Egypt (c. 1550–1070 BCE), prices were stated in copper weights called deben but paid in goods; the tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina wrote their deals on ostraca.
currencies.source_title: Prices of Commodities (Encyclopedia.com)
currencies.noun_fit: Cats were household favourites in ancient Egypt, and the village's sketches on ostraca include them.

currencies.name: Amole Bar
currencies.line: A bar of rock salt as small change, worth more the farther it went.
currencies.how: Bars are earned by carrying goods to members who live farther away and spent on grain, cloth or a hand with chores. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Rectangular bars of rock salt called amole served as money across Ethiopia for centuries and still circulated in the early 20th century, buying more the farther they travelled from the salt flats.
currencies.source_title: Ethiopia, 1 amoli – National Currency Collection (Bank of Canada Museum)
currencies.noun_fit: Amole bars were pocket change, and a wallet with a watchful eye is where you would keep them.

currencies.name: Copper Cross
currencies.line: Cast copper crosses that travelled as a store of value.
currencies.how: Crosses are earned by mending tools or recycling metal for the group and spent on food, tools or repairs from other members. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Smiths in Katanga cast copper in sand moulds as X- or H-shaped handa ingots that circulated across southern Central Africa in the 19th and early 20th centuries; many were recycled into wire.
currencies.source_title: Currency (handas) 'Katanga Cross' (Herbert F. Johnson Museum of Art, Cornell University)
currencies.noun_fit: Many crosses ended up drawn into copper wire, and a retainer is mostly neatly bent wire.

currencies.name: Dhofar Resin
currencies.line: Frankincense from Dhofar's groves, traded for cloth, grain and oil.
currencies.how: Tears are earned by tending a shared garden or orchard and spent on cloth, food or help from other members. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From antiquity to the late medieval period, Dhofar shipped frankincense; the 1st-century Periplus describes ships from India bringing cloth, grain and oil to trade for it at Moscha (Khor Rori).
currencies.source_title: Land of Frankincense (UNESCO World Heritage Centre)
currencies.noun_fit: Frankincense was a luxury of the ancient world's perfume and beauty trade, and lipstick is its modern cousin on the shelf.

currencies.name: Maize Bucket
currencies.line: When cash failed, rural households traded livestock for maize.
currencies.how: In a lean season, Buckets are earned by bringing grain or animal care to a community storehouse and spent on staples or help. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: During Zimbabwe's 2007–2009 hyperinflation, rural households in Matabeleland bartered goats, chickens and cattle for buckets of maize as cash lost its value, IRIN reported.
currencies.source_title: Zimbabwe: Farm animals bartered to stave off hunger (IRIN / The New Humanitarian)
currencies.noun_fit: Chosen for the chicken on its chest, which stands for the hens that, with goats and cattle, became households' store of value.

currencies.name: Coastal Voucher
currencies.line: Community-issued vouchers circulating beside the shilling.
currencies.how: Households and community groups earn Vouchers by trading goods or help with neighbours and spend them the same way, on a public, interest-free ledger. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Since 2010 the Kenyan organisation Grassroots Economics has supported community voucher networks, now called Sarafu; a peer-reviewed dataset logs about 55,000 accounts in 2020–2021.
currencies.source_title: Sarafu Community Inclusion Currency 2020–2021 (Scientific Data)
currencies.noun_fit: Zebras roam Kenya's plains, and their black-and-white stripes look like a ledger of credits and debits.

currencies.name: Okaz Verse
currencies.line: A seasonal fair where tribes traded goods and poets competed.
currencies.how: Verses are earned by bringing crafts or performing at a seasonal fair and spent on goods or skills on offer there. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Souq Okaz near Taif was Arabia's best-known seasonal fair from pre-Islamic times until the 8th century, where tribes traded goods and poets competed; Saudi Arabia revived it as a festival in 2007.
currencies.source_title: Souk Okaz Festival (Saudipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Okaz was as famous for spoken poetry as for trade, so a speech bubble fits.

currencies.name: Dilmun Pearl
currencies.line: An island harbour linking Mesopotamia, Oman and the Indus.
currencies.how: Pearls are earned by relaying goods between a network's member groups and spent on goods any member offers. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Qal'at al-Bahrain was the capital and harbour of Dilmun (c. 2300–1600 BCE), where merchants from Ur paid in textiles, grain and oil for copper from Magan and goods from the Indus.
currencies.source_title: Qal'at al-Bahrain – Ancient Harbour and Capital of Dilmun (UNESCO World Heritage Centre)
currencies.noun_fit: Bahrain's waters have been famous for pearl oysters since antiquity, so Dilmun gets the oyster.

currencies.name: Barley Measure
currencies.line: Barley and silver as the yardstick for wages, goods and debts.
currencies.how: Measures are earned by growing, milling or baking for the group and spent on food or help; prices are set in Measures, not cash. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In ancient Mesopotamia, barley and weighed silver were the yardsticks for goods, wages and debts, often paid in kind; law codes fixed equivalents, and silver coils were snipped to settle debts.
currencies.source_title: Oriental Institute exhibit examines commerce, trade in ancient Near East (University of Chicago News)
currencies.noun_fit: Mesopotamia's barley was also brewed into beer, and beer rations were a common way to pay workers.

currencies.name: Tan-Tan Moussem
currencies.line: A yearly gathering of Saharan nomads to trade, race and recite.
currencies.how: Tents are earned by hosting, cooking or bringing goods to a yearly gathering and spent on food, crafts or help there. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The Moussem of Tan-Tan, held since 1963 (paused 1979–2004), gathers Saharan nomadic peoples to buy, sell and exchange goods; UNESCO inscribed it as intangible heritage in 2008.
currencies.source_title: Moussem of Tan-Tan (UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage)
currencies.noun_fit: A scorpion is a desert native, at home where the moussem's nomadic peoples gather.

currencies.name: İmece Harvest
currencies.line: Village hands pooled for harvests, winter stores and building.
currencies.how: Neighbours earn Hands by joining a harvest, a winter-food day or a building job, and spend them to call a crew to their own task. Hands are never bought or cashed out, and the host still feeds the crew.
currencies.fact: İmece is a long-standing Anatolian village custom: neighbours pool unpaid labour for a household's harvest, winter food or building, the help is returned, and the host feeds the crew.
currencies.source_title: A Perspective on 'Imece' and 'Cooperative' Culture in Turks (FAO AGRIS record, Sinop University study)
currencies.noun_fit: A scorpion's eight legs carry one body in step, like an imece crew moving across one household's field.

currencies.name: Grain de Sel
currencies.line: Neighbours swap skills and goods, logged in 'grains of salt'.
currencies.how: Members earn Grains by offering services, skills or goods listed in the local catalogue and spend them on other members' offers. Grains are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: France's first système d'échange local started in Ariège in 1994, adapting Canada's LETS; hundreds followed, recording members' exchanges in local units often called grains de sel.
currencies.source_title: Les systèmes d'échanges locaux (doctoral thesis, Université de Bordeaux, 2015; theses.fr)
currencies.noun_fit: A film canister is the classic pocket jar for small grains, here a few grains of salt.

currencies.name: Auzolan Stone
currencies.line: Every household lends a hand to keep roads and fountains going.
currencies.how: Stones are earned by giving labour or materials to a shared path, fountain or garden and spent on help for your household. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Auzolan is the Basque custom of neighbourhood work: each household gave labour, and sometimes money for materials, to build and maintain roads, fountains, churches and forest trails.
currencies.source_title: Communal work (Basque Ethnography at a Glance, Labayru Fundazioa)
currencies.noun_fit: Read it as plumbing: a pipe for the fountains and water channels that neighbours kept running.

currencies.name: Brighton Seed
currencies.line: Growers bring home-saved seeds to a big February swap table.
currencies.how: Packets are earned by bringing home-saved seeds to a swap table and spent on other growers' seeds or seedlings. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Seedy Sunday has been held in Brighton and Hove since 2002, inspired by a Vancouver event; growers swap home-saved seeds each February, and organisers call it the UK's biggest seed swap.
currencies.source_title: Seedy Sunday – seed swap & sale (Brighton & Hove Food Partnership)
currencies.noun_fit: Brighton is a seaside city, and the rainbow on this shark's body nods to its famous Pride.

currencies.name: Talkoot Call
currencies.line: Villagers and club members gather to finish a job together.
currencies.how: Berries are earned by joining a village or club work day, from fixing a hall to staffing a kiosk, and spent on help with your own project. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Talkoot is a centuries-old Finnish form of voluntary collective work, from renovating village halls to yard clean-ups; it is recorded in the Finnish Heritage Agency's living heritage wiki-inventory.
currencies.source_title: Talkoot work tradition (Wiki-inventory for Living Heritage, Finnish Heritage Agency)
currencies.noun_fit: Finland's forests are full of wild blueberries, the country's favourite free harvest.

currencies.name: Vaðmál Ell
currencies.line: Standard homespun wool, measured in ells, paid for prices and taxes.
currencies.how: Ells are earned by spinning, weaving, knitting or mending for the group and spent on goods or help from other members. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From about the 12th to the 17th century, Iceland used a legally standardised homespun woollen cloth, vaðmál, measured in ells, to pay prices and taxes; women did most of the production.
currencies.source_title: Silver, Butter, Cloth: Monetary and Social Economies in the Viking Age (Oxford University Press)
currencies.noun_fit: Lint is what woven wool leaves behind, a fluffy tribute to the women who made the cloth.

currencies.name: Winter Market
currencies.line: A February market reached along frozen rivers in Lapland.
currencies.how: Sleds are earned by bringing handmade goods or food to a winter market and spent on other makers' wares. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Jokkmokk's winter market has been held each February since 1605, when the Swedish crown set up marketplaces near Sámi winter settlements; it remains a major Sámi gathering and craft market.
currencies.source_title: History (Jokkmokks marknad, official site)
currencies.noun_fit: A snow-white, ice-cold Noun for a market whose first traders travelled on frozen rivers.

currencies.name: Kaláka Raising
currencies.line: Neighbours raise a house, and now village baths, together.
currencies.how: Beams are earned by giving a day to a neighbour's build or a shared village project and spent when you need a crew in turn. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Kaláka is the long-standing Hungarian and Székely voluntary work party; since 2001 a kaláka movement that began in Lázárfalva has built village baths and community spaces.
currencies.source_title: 25 years of the kaláka movement (Pesti Vigadó, Hungarian Academy of Arts)
currencies.noun_fit: Hungarian folk music has its own bagpipe, the duda, and the snowflake on its chest suits Transylvanian winters.

currencies.name: Swish Party
currencies.line: Bring a good garment, leave with someone else's.
currencies.how: Garments are earned by bringing good-quality clothes or accessories to a swap party and spent on other guests' pieces; leftovers go to charity. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In 2000 the London sustainability agency Futerra gave the name swishing to clothes-swap parties, where guests bring good-quality clothes and take home others'; the format spread across the UK.
currencies.source_title: Swish till you drop (Down To Earth)
currencies.noun_fit: Every swish has a shoe rail, and a high heel is its star.

currencies.name: Ecoxarxa Fair
currencies.tradition: Ecoxarxes (Catalan eco-networks) and social-currency barter fairs
currencies.line: Eco-networks trading at barter fairs in their own social currency.
currencies.how: Baskets are earned by bringing food, crafts or services to a seasonal barter fair and spent on other stallholders' goods. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Catalonia's ecoxarxes appeared around 2009 in places such as Montseny, each with its own social currency; in September 2010 Barcelona's Ecoxarxa held the city's first barter fair using one.
currencies.source_title: Barcelona farà la primera fira d'intercanvi amb moneda social (Nació Digital, Sept 2010)
currencies.noun_fit: Catalan cooks pound garlic into allioli, so a bulb is at home at a Catalan fair.

currencies.name: Dugnad Day
currencies.line: Unpaid shared work for the co-op, the school and the club.
currencies.how: Brushes are earned by joining a clean-up, painting day or repair session for a shared building, school or club and spent on help from other members. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Dugnad, from Old Norse dugnaðr ('help'), is Norway's tradition of voluntary communal work, rooted in farm communities and now how housing co-ops, schools and clubs get jobs done.
currencies.source_title: dugnad (Store norske leksikon)
currencies.noun_fit: A housing co-op's dugnad means scrubbing the shared spaces, so the washing machine gets to work.

currencies.name: Meitheal Sheaf
currencies.line: Neighbours saving hay and cutting turf together, repaid in help.
currencies.how: Sheaves are earned by joining a neighbour's heavy seasonal job, such as bringing in a garden or moving house, and spent when you need a crew. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Meitheal, the Irish work party, saw neighbours join forces to save hay, thresh and cut turf until machinery took over in the mid-20th century; help was repaid with help, not money.
currencies.source_title: Meitheal: A Study of Co-operative Labour in Rural Ireland (Four Courts Press / Folklore of Ireland Council)
currencies.noun_fit: Bringing home the harvest was often marked with a house dance, and Ireland has its own bagpipes, the uilleann pipes.

currencies.name: Factory Swap
currencies.line: Cash-short factories paid one another in goods and offsets.
currencies.how: Makerspace members earn Wagons by sharing offcuts, tools or materials with other members and spend them on what they need, with a public ledger keeping chains clear. Wagons are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In 1990s Russia, cash-short enterprises paid each other in kind; barter and other non-cash deals rose from under 10% of industrial sales in 1992 to over half by August 1998, then fell.
currencies.source_title: Barter in Russia: Liquidity Shortage versus Lack of Restructuring (University of Michigan Deep Blue)
currencies.noun_fit: Energy and raw materials were among the goods swapped, so the pipe stands in for the pipelines.

currencies.name: Sardinian Circuit
currencies.line: Island traders on a zero-interest credit ledger.
currencies.how: Neighbours earn Loops by offering skills or goods to other members and spend them inside the circuit, with no interest either way. Loops are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Launched in 2009 in Serramanna by five young founders who modelled it on Switzerland's WIR, Sardex lets Sardinian businesses trade on a mutual-credit ledger at 0% interest.
currencies.source_title: From complementary currency to institution: a micro-macro study of the Sardex mutual credit system (LSE Research Online)
currencies.noun_fit: An Italian circuit gets the most Italian dish in the Nouns kitchen, sliced so everyone gets a piece.

currencies.name: Toloka Wall
currencies.line: Villagers raise clay-and-straw walls together, then celebrate.
currencies.how: Daubs are earned by joining a group build or repair day and spent when your own home or garden needs many hands. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Toloka is an old Ukrainian custom of collective village work, from harvests to raising houses with clay-straw walls; ethnographers record building tolokas and their rites into the 20th century.
currencies.source_title: The Ethnology Notebooks, 2025 No. 2 (182), Institute of Ethnology, NAS of Ukraine
currencies.noun_fit: Clay and straw for the walls were often mixed underfoot, so the toloka gets a sturdy boot.

currencies.name: Pomor Cod
currencies.line: Russian rye flour for Norwegian cod along the Arctic coast.
currencies.how: Barrels are earned by bringing surplus fish, flour or preserves to a coastal swap and spent on what neighbours across the water produce. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From about 1740 to 1917, Pomors from Russia's White Sea coast sailed to northern Norway to trade rye flour and grain for fish, mainly cod; the trade ended with the 1917 Revolution.
currencies.source_title: Pomor trade (Northern Lights, UiT The Arctic University of Norway Library)
currencies.noun_fit: Whales feed in the same cold, fish-rich Arctic waters the Pomor ships crossed.

currencies.name: Volos Exchange
currencies.tradition: TEM of the Magnesia Exchange and Solidarity Network
currencies.line: Residents trading on a shared ledger as austerity cut incomes.
currencies.how: Residents earn Olives by offering goods or services on a shared online ledger and spend them on other members' offers, with no interest on balances. Olives are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The TEM network began in Volos in 2010 as Greece's debt crisis cut incomes; members trade on an online ledger in units valued at one euro, and within a year it had hundreds of members.
currencies.source_title: Modern Greeks Return To Ancient System Of Barter (NPR, 29 Nov 2011)
currencies.noun_fit: A second calculator for a second ledger, this one kept by neighbours through hard times.

currencies.name: Basel Ring
currencies.line: Firms kept trading on book-entry credit through the 1930s slump.
currencies.how: Members earn Rings by offering goods or skills to others in the circle and spend them inside it, so the ledger always nets to zero. Rings are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Founded in Zurich in 1934 by businessmen including Werner Zimmermann and Paul Enz, the WIR cooperative let firms short of francs trade in book-entry units; it runs today as WIR Bank in Basel.
currencies.source_title: Cash substitute greases business wheels (swissinfo.ch)
currencies.noun_fit: Mutual credit is ledger arithmetic, so the circle that started it all gets a calculator.

currencies.name: Butter and Grain
currencies.line: Grain, butter and cloth traded directly in a Himalayan kingdom.
currencies.how: Bushels are earned by bringing grain, dairy or woven goods to a village exchange and spent on other households' produce or help. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Indian and Bhutanese coins circulated in Bhutan, but until the 1960s most transactions were barter; a decimal rupee became standard in 1957, and the ngultrum replaced it in 1974.
currencies.source_title: Bhutan: Currency (Library of Congress Country Studies)
currencies.noun_fit: Bhutan is a Himalayan kingdom, so its note wears a crown.

currencies.name: Bamboo Shoot
currencies.line: City families shed valuables layer by layer for rice.
currencies.how: Layers are earned by bringing clothing or household goods to a community exchange and spent on food from local growers. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In Japan's food shortages after 1945, city dwellers traded kimono and valuables to farmers for rice; it was called takenoko seikatsu, 'bamboo-shoot living', like a shoot shedding its sheaths.
currencies.source_title: Occupied Japan 1945–1952: Gender, Class, Race (University of Maryland MITH archive)
currencies.noun_fit: A folding fan stands in for the kimono and household treasures families gave up one layer at a time.

currencies.name: Hanbat Circle
currencies.line: Neighbours trading goods, services and labour on a local ledger.
currencies.how: Members earn Spoons by offering goods, services or labour to each other and spend them on members' offers; balances carry no interest. Spoons are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Hanbat LETS in Daejeon, running since about 2000, lets members trade goods, services and labour in a community unit called the duru; it is studied as a leading Korean community currency.
currencies.source_title: Local currencies make happy cities (Korea JoongAng Daily)
currencies.noun_fit: Korean cooking runs on garlic, so a bulb is at home in a Korean exchange.

currencies.name: Dolpo Salt
currencies.line: Yak caravans carrying Tibetan salt south for hill-grown grain.
currencies.how: Loads are earned by hauling goods up or down the valley for neighbours and spent on grain, wool or help. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: For centuries Dolpo's agro-pastoralists carried Tibetan salt south by yak and sheep caravan to barter for grain; the trade shrank after the 1959 border closure, but smaller caravans continue.
currencies.source_title: The cultural ecology of yak production in Dolpo, West Nepal (ILRI yak conference proceedings)
currencies.noun_fit: A ski lift for a trade that has always had to climb over high Himalayan passes.

currencies.name: Attam Paddy
currencies.line: A day in your paddy repaid with a day in mine.
currencies.how: Furrows are earned by working a day in another member's garden or field and spent on an equal day of help in yours. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Attam is a reciprocal labour exchange in Sinhalese paddy villages, repaid day for day in labour; 1970s–80s studies recorded its decline as wage labour spread, though it survives in places.
currencies.source_title: Traditional exchange-labour in hill country Sri Lanka: A study of the attam institution (NSF Sri Lanka digital library)
currencies.noun_fit: Frogs are paddy-field regulars, and the infinity sign on its chest suits a favour that keeps going round.

currencies.name: Kota Belud Tamu
currencies.line: A weekly meeting place for seafarers, farmers and traders.
currencies.how: Stalls are earned by bringing produce, crafts or fish to a weekly market and spent on goods from other communities. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Sabah's tamu are periodic markets where seafarers, traders and farmers met to swap produce; Kota Belud's, begun at Tempasuk in 1878, still draws Bajau, Dusun and Iranun communities weekly.
currencies.source_title: Tamu (Weekly Market) in Sabah (Sabah Tourism Board)
currencies.noun_fit: Kota Belud is known for its horses, and the unicorn is the most dazzling horse in the Nouns stable.

currencies.name: Tea Brick
currencies.line: Compressed tea bricks, scored so pieces could break off as change.
currencies.how: Bricks are earned by preparing food and drink for shared gatherings and spent on goods or help; a Brick splits into small pieces for little trades. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Into the 20th century, and in Siberia until about World War II, compressed tea bricks served as money across Mongolia, Tibet and Siberia; they were scored so pieces could be broken off as change.
currencies.source_title: Tea brick currency (Bank of Canada Museum)
currencies.noun_fit: The first handheld game consoles were nicknamed 'the brick', which makes this the perfect tea brick.

currencies.name: Jonbeel Fair
currencies.line: Hill produce traded for plains rice cakes, without cash.
currencies.how: Pithas are earned by bringing produce, mats or snacks to a yearly fair and spent on goods from the other side of the valley. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Each January at Dayang Belguri, near Jagiroad, Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and other hill communities barter ginger, lac and mats with plains villagers for rice cakes and dried fish.
currencies.source_title: Barter trade conducted on 2nd day at Jonbeel Mela (The Assam Tribune)
currencies.noun_fit: Jonbeel means 'moon wetland', after the crescent-shaped lake beside the fair.

currencies.name: Caring Ticket
currencies.line: Hours of help for older people, saved for later or sent to family.
currencies.how: Visits are earned by helping older neighbours with shopping, housework or company and can be saved for your own care or passed to a relative. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Fureai Kippu, a Japanese time-credit scheme since 1995, lets volunteers earn credits helping older people and save or transfer them; it grew from an Osaka volunteer labour bank begun in 1973.
currencies.source_title: Japan's Fureai Kippu Time-banking in Elderly Care (International Journal of Community Currency Research)
currencies.noun_fit: Caring for older people often starts with a pill organiser, so the pill suits a scheme built on care.

currencies.name: Anyui Fair
currencies.line: A river fair where Chukchi traders met Russian merchants.
currencies.how: Kettles are earned by bringing tools, food or crafts to a yearly river fair and spent on other traders' goods. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From 1788/89 an annual fair at the Anyuysky fort on the Maly Anyuy River brought Chukchi traders and Russian merchants together, exchanging furs and walrus ivory for tea, tobacco and iron tools.
currencies.source_title: Russian Museum of Ethnography online catalogue: article on the Anyui fair
currencies.noun_fit: Red and silver fox furs were among the goods Chukchi traders brought to the fair.

currencies.name: Prahok Season
currencies.tradition: Rice-for-fish trade of the prahok season
currencies.line: Farmers bring rice to the river and leave with fish for prahok.
currencies.how: Jars are earned by bringing grain, or by helping neighbours clean and pack fish for their own households, and spent on fish or preserved food. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Each dry season, Cambodian farmers travel to the Tonle Sap River's dai fisheries to trade rice or cash for small fish to ferment into prahok; some fish workers are paid in rice.
currencies.source_title: Prahoc Season Brings Flood Of Villagers to Dai Fisheries (The Cambodia Daily)
currencies.noun_fit: Fish on rice: nigiri is the whole prahok trade in one bite.

currencies.name: Đổi Công Day
currencies.line: Households trade days of labour for transplanting and harvest.
currencies.how: Paddies are earned by working a day in a neighbour's field or at a family occasion and spent when you need extra hands. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In northern Vietnam's rice villages, households exchange days of labour for transplanting, harvesting and family occasions; one field study found it the most common collective farm work.
currencies.source_title: Aide et entraide agricole dans un village du Nord-Viêt-nam (Aséanie, via HAL)
currencies.noun_fit: Northern Vietnam's rice becomes its famous rice noodles, so the bowl suits a rice-village exchange.

currencies.name: Yui Thatch
currencies.era: Edo era to now; ledger from 1792
currencies.line: Neighbours re-thatch a steep roof in a day, logged in a ledger.
currencies.how: Bundles are earned by giving labour or materials to a neighbour's big repair, recorded in a shared ledger, and spent when your turn comes. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In Shirakawa-go's gassho-zukuri villages, yui is mutual help to re-thatch roofs every 20–30 years; each household's labour, thatch and sake went in a yui-cho ledger, the oldest from 1792.
currencies.source_title: Yui and the Village Community (Japan Tourism Agency / MLIT multilingual database)
currencies.noun_fit: A freshly thatched roof looks a lot like a thick head of hair.

currencies.name: Asar Call
currencies.line: Relatives and neighbours raise a yurt or a house together.
currencies.how: Yurts are earned by joining a big household job, such as building, haymaking or shearing, and spent when you need a crew; the host provides a meal. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Asar is a Kazakh custom in which relatives and neighbours do work too big for one household, such as building, raising a yurt, haymaking or shearing; it is unpaid, and the host offers a meal.
currencies.source_title: Asar – tradition of the joint collaborative labor (e-history.kz)
currencies.noun_fit: On the steppe, horses matter most, and the unicorn is the Nouns' horse; the heart is for neighbourly help.

currencies.name: Sulu Sea Barter
currencies.line: Seaweed and farm goods swapped across an old sea border.
currencies.how: Bales are earned by bringing marine or farm produce to a port swap and spent on household goods from partner communities. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Barter across the Sulu Sea between the southern Philippines, Sabah and Indonesia predates modern borders; Executive Order 64 of 2018 revived and regulated it at ports in Jolo, Siasi and Bongao.
currencies.source_title: Executive Order No. 64, s. 2018 – Mindanao Barter Council (LawPhil)
currencies.noun_fit: A sea creature with an anchor on its chest, for trade that docks at island ports.

currencies.name: Wulandoni Market
currencies.line: Coastal fish and salt traded for upland maize and bananas.
currencies.how: Bunches are earned by bringing fish, salt or crops to a weekly market and spent on goods from the other side of the island, at rates the community agrees. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: At Wulandoni's weekly market on Lembata, coastal women trade fish, salt and lime with upland villagers for maize, bananas and cassava, mostly without money and at customary rates.
currencies.source_title: Barter Transactions at the Wulandoni Market (Sodality, IPB University)
currencies.noun_fit: A small coastal fish, the kind of catch that changes hands at Wulandoni.

currencies.name: Tea Horse Road
currencies.line: Brick tea carried over mountain routes in exchange for horses.
currencies.how: Packs are earned by carrying or delivering goods over long distances for the network and spent on goods or rides from members along the route. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From at least the Song dynasty, Chinese states traded compressed tea from Yunnan and Sichuan for Tibetan horses; National Geographic reports about 25,000 horses a year by the 13th century.
currencies.source_title: Tea Horse (National Geographic Magazine, May 2010)
currencies.noun_fit: It is right there in the name: the Tea Horse Road.

currencies.name: Trepang Season
currencies.line: Makassar crews traded cloth and tools for access to trepang.
currencies.how: Praus are earned by sharing local knowledge or help with visiting crews and spent on the tools, cloth or food they bring. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: For generations until 1907, prau crews from Makassar sailed to Arnhem Land to harvest and process trepang, giving Yolŋu people cloth, tobacco, rice and metal tools for access and help.
currencies.source_title: Trade with Makasar – Defining Moments (National Museum of Australia)
currencies.noun_fit: A trepang, or sea cucumber, looks remarkably like a pickle.

currencies.name: Bunya Gathering
currencies.line: Nations gathered whenever the bunya pines cropped heavily.
currencies.how: Cones are earned by bringing food, tools or skills to a seasonal gathering and spent on what other groups bring. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: About every three years, when bunya pines cropped heavily, Aboriginal nations met in the Bunya Mountains to feast, trade and settle disputes; the last known was in 1902, and it is being revived.
currencies.source_title: Bunya governance (Office of the Registrar of Indigenous Corporations, Australian Government)
currencies.noun_fit: Bunya pines belong to an ancient lineage that reaches back to the age of the dinosaurs.

currencies.name: Crop Swap
currencies.line: Neighbours swap surplus homegrown produce as fuel prices bite.
currencies.how: Punnets are earned by bringing surplus homegrown fruit, vegetables or herbs to a swap and spent on other growers' produce. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Since fuel prices spiked in March 2026, the Comboyne Farm Store has hosted crop swaps where residents trade surplus homegrown produce; a crop swap in Forster has drawn about 300 people.
currencies.source_title: Communities turn to barter-style crop swaps to combat cost-of-living crisis (ABC News, 28 June 2026)
currencies.noun_fit: A garden gnome guards the backyard veggie patch where all the swap produce grows.

currencies.name: Solesolevaki Work
currencies.line: Villagers pool unpaid labour for the common good.
currencies.how: Posts record contributions to shared projects, such as rebuilding after a storm, and are spent on group help for any household in need, serving the common good rather than paying individuals. Never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Solesolevaki is the iTaukei custom of unpaid communal work for shared goals such as building and farming; UNDP documented it uniting Kadavu villagers and kin abroad to rebuild after a cyclone.
currencies.source_title: When disaster hits, solesolevaki fights back (UNDP Pacific)
currencies.noun_fit: An island in a safety vest: Kadavu's villagers rebuilding together after a cyclone.

currencies.name: Island Seed Swap
currencies.line: Farmers and gardeners swap seeds of locally adapted crops.
currencies.how: Cuttings are earned by bringing clean, pest-free seeds or cuttings to a swap and spent on other growers' varieties. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Hawaiʻi Island's first community seed exchange was held in Kona in 2002; later swaps with partners such as The Kohala Center let growers trade seeds and cuttings of locally adapted food crops.
currencies.source_title: Seed exchange gives gardeners a wide variety of choices (Hawaii Tribune-Herald, 11 April 2016)
currencies.noun_fit: Hawaiʻi Island was built by volcanoes, and its gardens grow in volcanic soil.

currencies.name: Saltwater Market
currencies.line: Lagoon fish traded for inland taro, yams and almonds.
currencies.how: Nets are earned by bringing fish or garden food to a boundary market and spent on what the other community grows or catches. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: On north-east Malaita, the Lau 'saltwater people' bartered fish and marine products with inland 'bush people' for taro, yams, Canarium almonds and forest goods at coastal markets.
currencies.source_title: Malaita (Encyclopedia of World Cultures, Encyclopedia.com)
currencies.noun_fit: A lagoon-and-reef creature for the saltwater side of the market.

currencies.name: Harbour Hour
currencies.line: A town time bank that held firm through the earthquakes.
currencies.how: Tides are earned by giving an hour of help to a neighbour or local group and spent on an hour of someone else's help. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Lyttelton's time bank, run by Project Lyttelton since the mid-2000s, is called New Zealand's first; in the 2010–11 earthquakes its network helped residents repair, feed and house each other.
currencies.source_title: The Lyttelton Timebank (University of Canterbury research impact)
currencies.noun_fit: After the Canterbury earthquakes, road cones became the region's unofficial emblem.

currencies.name: Maleny Exchange
currencies.line: Australia's first LETS, trading in a local unit called the bunya.
currencies.how: Members earn Sparks by offering goods or services to neighbours, recorded as credits, and spend them on other members' offers. Sparks are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Started in 1987 by residents inspired by Canada's Comox Valley LETS, Maleny's Local Energy Transfer System is widely cited as Australia's first; members trade in a local unit, the bunya.
currencies.source_title: Williams (1997), International Journal of Community Currency Research, Vol. 1
currencies.noun_fit: Here LETS stands for Local Energy Transfer System, so a bolt of energy fits.

currencies.name: Wairarapa Green
currencies.line: A rural mutual-credit exchange for local goods and services.
currencies.how: Members earn Vines by trading local goods and services, recorded in member accounts, and spend them at markets or with other members. Vines are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Formed in 1991 as a LETS, the Wairarapa Green Dollar Exchange trades in a mutual-credit unit called the WAIS, worth about one NZ dollar; since 2008, vouchers have let non-members take part.
currencies.source_title: Origins in the Wairarapa (Wairarapa Green Dollar Exchange)
currencies.noun_fit: The Wairarapa is one of New Zealand's best-known wine regions.

currencies.name: Fish for Sago
currencies.tradition: Fish-for-sago barter markets of the Middle Sepik
currencies.line: River women traded fish for sago at markets reached by canoe.
currencies.how: Canoes are earned by bringing fresh or smoked food to a regular market and spent on staples from neighbouring villages. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Iatmul women of the Middle Sepik traditionally bartered fresh and smoked fish for sago from neighbouring Sawos villages at regular women's markets, an exchange recorded through the 20th century.
currencies.source_title: Iatmul (Encyclopedia of World Cultures, Encyclopedia.com)
currencies.noun_fit: A soft white steamed bun is the closest Noun to a cake of sago starch.

currencies.name: Hiri Voyage
currencies.place: Port Moresby to Gulf of Papua, PNG
currencies.line: Clay pots sailed west by lakatoi and traded for sago.
currencies.how: Sails are earned by making or carrying goods for a seasonal swap between two communities and spent on staples the other side produces. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Each year Motu men sailed lakatoi canoes up to about 400 km west carrying clay pots made by Motu women, which Gulf of Papua communities traded for sago and canoe logs.
currencies.source_title: Historicizing Motu ceramics and the hiri trade (James Cook University ResearchOnline)
currencies.noun_fit: A pie dish is a fair stand-in for a clay pot, and the anchor on its chest is for the voyage.

currencies.name: Siassi Voyager
currencies.line: Seafaring middlemen turning taro into pots, and pots into pigs.
currencies.how: Bowls are earned by carrying goods between partner communities and spent on goods anywhere along the chain. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Siassi Islanders were seafaring middlemen linking New Guinea's north coast with Umboi and New Britain; Thomas Harding's 1967 study traced value converted from taro to pots to pigs.
currencies.source_title: Lilley (2007), Technical Reports of the Australian Museum Online 20 (Australian Museum)
currencies.noun_fit: Value took winding routes through this network, from taro to pots to pigs, like a maze.

currencies.name: Island Barter
currencies.line: A no-cash barter group that grew as jobs vanished in 2020.
currencies.how: Parcels are earned by offering food, plants, crafts or labour in a no-cash swap group and spent on other members' offers. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Suva resident Marlene Dutta launched the Facebook group Barter for Better Fiji in April 2020 after COVID-19 job losses; it grew to well over 100,000 members swapping food, crafts and labour.
currencies.source_title: Bartering through the pandemic in Fiji (Pacific Community SPC GEM blog, November 2021)
currencies.noun_fit: In 2020 household essentials became prized swaps, and the heart on this roll is for neighbours helping neighbours.

currencies.name: Tītī for Kūmara
currencies.tradition: Kaihaukai food exchange: tītī for kūmara
currencies.line: Southern muttonbirds exchanged for kūmara grown in the north.
currencies.how: Gourds are earned by preserving or growing food for a partner community and spent on what grows best in theirs; each gift invites an equal or better one. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Southern iwi preserved tītī (muttonbirds) in kelp bags and exchanged them for kūmara and other foods from the north; Te Ara notes that such gifts called for an equal or better return, building mana.
currencies.source_title: Te mahi kai – food production economics (Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand)
currencies.noun_fit: Hue, the gourds that travelled south in these exchanges, are cousins of the pumpkin.

currencies.name: Strait Visit
currencies.tradition: Traditional barter under the Torres Strait Treaty
currencies.line: Customary barter protected across an international border.
currencies.how: Dinghies are earned by bringing customary goods to visiting neighbours and spent on what they bring in turn; non-commercial only. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The 1978 Torres Strait Treaty between Australia and Papua New Guinea, in force since 1985, protects 'barter and market trade' as a traditional activity of the Strait's traditional inhabitants.
currencies.source_title: Guidelines for traditional visitors travelling under the Torres Strait Treaty (Australian DFAT)
currencies.noun_fit: Islands are the stepping stones of the Strait, and the rings on its chest stand for ties across the water.

currencies.name: Gimwali Market
currencies.tradition: Gimwali barter alongside the kula ring
currencies.line: Everyday haggling barter that runs beside the ceremonial kula.
currencies.how: Yams are earned by bringing food or crafts to a market day and spent on other islanders' goods; they cover everyday barter only, never ceremonial gifts. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The kula is ceremonial exchange: partners pass named shell valuables around a ring of islands for prestige. Trobriand Islanders keep it apart from gimwali, the ordinary haggling barter of goods.
currencies.source_title: Reciprocity & Exchange: The Kula Ring (Human Relations Area Files, Yale University)
currencies.noun_fit: Saturn's ring echoes the ring of islands that kula voyages travel, where gimwali barter goes on alongside.

currencies.name: Barter Ticket
currencies.line: Depression audiences paid for theatre seats with farm produce.
currencies.how: Seats are earned by bringing food or volunteering for a community stage and spent on performances, workshops or snacks. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Actor Robert Porterfield opened Barter Theatre in 1933; Depression audiences could pay admission in produce, and actors were paid partly in food. It is now the State Theatre of Virginia.
currencies.source_title: Barter Theatre (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Show business: the reel of film stands in for the footlights.

currencies.name: Ayni Terrace
currencies.line: Help with planting today, the same help in kind tomorrow.
currencies.how: Terraces are earned by helping a household with planting, harvest or building and spent on the same kind and amount of help later. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Ayni is the Andean principle of reciprocity: one household helps another with planting, harvest or building and later receives the same help in kind. It predates the Inca and continues today.
currencies.source_title: Ayni (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Ayni gives back exactly what was given, a reflection in kind.

currencies.name: Trafkintu Seeds
currencies.tradition: Trafkintu (Mapuche exchange of seeds and goods)
currencies.line: Families exchange seeds, potatoes and foods to renew their stock.
currencies.how: Seedlings are earned by bringing native seeds, plants or foods to an exchange gathering and spent on other families' varieties. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Trafkintu is a Mapuche practice of exchanging seeds, plants and foods between families and communities; in recent decades it has been revived as gatherings that conserve native crop varieties.
currencies.source_title: Trafkintu (Wikipedia, español)
currencies.noun_fit: Garlic is grown from saved cloves, and the rainbow on its chest stands for the many native varieties shared.

currencies.name: Club de Trueque
currencies.line: Neighbourhood barter clubs that spread through a national crisis.
currencies.how: Nodos are earned by bringing homemade food, goods or services to a neighbourhood barter club and spent there, with issuance capped to members' trades. Never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The Red Global de Trueque began with a barter club in Bernal in 1995 and grew into a national network using paper créditos; it drew millions in the 2001–02 crisis, then collapsed amid over-issue.
currencies.source_title: Red Global de Trueque (Wikipedia, español)
currencies.noun_fit: A network that called itself 'global' gets a whole planet.

currencies.name: Minga de Tiradura
currencies.line: Neighbours and oxen haul a wooden house to its new home.
currencies.how: Oxen are earned by lending strength, tools or a team to a neighbour's big move and spent when your household needs a crew; the host serves a meal. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In Chiloé's minga de tiradura, neighbours move a family's wooden house on log rollers with ox teams, sometimes floating it across the water; the owners repay the help with a meal.
currencies.source_title: Minga (Wikipedia, español)
currencies.noun_fit: A house, mid-journey: the whole minga revolves around one.

currencies.name: Havana Permuta
currencies.line: Families swapped homes when they could not buy or sell them.
currencies.how: Keys are earned by opening your home for a swap or a stay and spent on a stay in another member's home. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: With home sales effectively banned after Cuba's 1960 Urban Reform, families moved by swapping homes in a permuta; a 2011 decree-law legalised sales, but the permuta remains a legal way to move.
currencies.source_title: Housing in Cuba (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Baseball is Havana's great passion, as much a part of the city as its permutas.

currencies.name: Made Beaver
currencies.line: Every kettle and blanket priced against one prime beaver pelt.
currencies.how: Goods are priced in Beavers, a fixed yardstick; members earn them by bringing goods or skills to a trading post and spend them on supplies. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From the late 17th century the Hudson's Bay Company priced furs and goods in Made Beaver, one prime processed beaver pelt; Cree and other Indigenous traders exchanged furs against this standard.
currencies.source_title: Made beaver (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Most beaver fur was felted into hats in Europe, so this note tops itself with one.

currencies.name: Knife River Flint
currencies.line: Village corn and squash traded for bison goods and horses.
currencies.how: Flints are earned by growing, gathering or making goods for a regional market and spent on goods from travelling partners. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: From about the 16th century to the 1840s, Hidatsa earth-lodge villages on the Knife River, near Mandan neighbours, were a Plains trade hub where corn and squash met bison goods and horses.
currencies.source_title: Knife River Indian Villages National Historic Site (National Park Service)
currencies.noun_fit: Knife River flint, the stone itself, was one of the villages' most prized trade goods.

currencies.name: Manka Fiesta
currencies.line: Highland pots, wool and salt bartered for valley maize and fruit.
currencies.how: Pots are earned by bringing crafts, wool or produce to a yearly border fair and spent on goods from other valleys. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Each October, La Quiaca's Manka Fiesta, named for the Quechua word for cooking pot, gathers potters, herders and farmers from the Puna and southern Bolivia to trade ceramics, wool and produce.
currencies.source_title: Manca Fiesta (Wikipedia, español)
currencies.noun_fit: A mug is a cooking pot's little cousin, fitting for a fair named after one.

currencies.name: Barn Raising
currencies.line: Neighbours frame and raise a barn in a day, help repaid later.
currencies.how: Pegs are earned by giving a day to a neighbour's big build or repair and spent when your own household needs a crew; the host provides meals. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In a barn raising, neighbours frame and raise a barn for one family in a day or two, common in rural North America in the 18th–19th centuries; Amish communities still do it as mutual aid.
currencies.source_title: Barn raising (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Barns are framed from timber, and the scissors on its chest hint at the cutting that comes first.

currencies.name: Grease Trail
currencies.tradition: Eulachon grease trade on the grease trails
currencies.line: Eulachon grease carried inland on foot for furs and hides.
currencies.how: Ladles are earned by preparing or carrying food between coastal and inland members and spent on goods from the other side. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Coastal peoples such as the Nuxalk rendered eulachon into a prized grease, carried inland on grease trails to trade with the Dakelh for furs and hides; Alexander Mackenzie followed one in 1793.
currencies.source_title: Grease trail (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Eulachon grease is a prized condiment on the coast, and the Nouns' condiment is a ketchup bottle.

currencies.name: Mutirão Build
currencies.line: Neighbours harvest, clear land or build homes together.
currencies.how: Tiles are earned by joining a neighbour's harvest or a group home build and spent when your household needs a crew; the host offers food. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Mutirão, from a Tupi word for collective work, is a Brazilian tradition of unpaid group efforts to harvest, clear land or build houses; it also underpins self-help housing mutirões in cities.
currencies.source_title: Mutirão (Wikipedia, português)
currencies.noun_fit: The pineapple is native to South America, and 'ananás' comes from Tupi, like mutirão itself.

currencies.name: Konbit Day
currencies.line: Neighbours work a field together to drums and song.
currencies.how: Hoes are earned by joining a neighbour's field day and spent when your own plot needs hands; the host provides the meal. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In a konbit, a Haitian work party since at least the 19th century, neighbours work one farmer's field together, often to drums, conch shells and work songs, while the host provides a meal.
currencies.source_title: Konbit (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Konbit work keeps rhythm with drums and song, so a music mixer sets the beat.

currencies.name: Self-Help Local
currencies.line: Jobless workers cut wood, fished and gleaned, then shared the take.
currencies.how: Cords are earned by gathering fuel or food, or gleaning surplus crops, for a community pantry and spent on what the pantry holds. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Formed in Seattle in 1931, the Unemployed Citizens' League organised jobless workers to cut firewood, fish and harvest unwanted crops in exchange for their labour, then shared the food and fuel.
currencies.source_title: The Great Depression in Washington State Project (University of Washington)
currencies.noun_fit: Puget Sound is orca country, and League members fished those same waters.

currencies.name: Cacao Bean
currencies.line: Cacao beans as small change in a market built on barter.
currencies.how: Beans are earned by bringing goods to a market swap, used as small change to even out trades, and spent on food or crafts. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In Aztec markets such as Tlatelolco, much trade was barter, with cacao beans as small change; a 16th-century record valued a turkey hen at 100 beans and a tamale at one.
currencies.source_title: A Brief History of Chocolate (Smithsonian Magazine)
currencies.noun_fit: The closest thing in the Nouns pantry to a cacao bean is its coffee-bean cousin.

currencies.name: Tallcan Trade
currencies.line: A no-cash swap scene where tallcans and transit tokens set prices.
currencies.how: Tokens are earned by offering household goods, clothes or furniture in a no-cash swap group and spent on other members' items. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Bunz Trading Zone began in Toronto in 2013 as a Facebook group with a no-cash rule; tall cans of beer, transit tokens and groceries became its informal units of exchange.
currencies.source_title: Bunz (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Bunz sounds like buns, and a hot dog is what goes in one.

currencies.name: Sunday Trueque
currencies.line: A Sunday market where produce and crafts trade without money.
currencies.how: Handfuls are earned by bringing produce, plants or crafts to a weekly market and spent on other families' goods. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Every Sunday the market in Zacualpan de Amilpas, Morelos, has a section where people still practise trueque, trading produce, plants and crafts without money, a custom traced to pre-Hispanic exchange.
currencies.source_title: Zacualpan de Amilpas (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Maize and beans fill the Sunday swap, and a taco wraps them both.

currencies.name: Fixers' Table
currencies.line: Volunteer fixers mend broken things alongside their owners.
currencies.how: Fixes are earned by volunteering repair skills or lending tools and spent on help mending your own broken item. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Former journalist Martine Postma organised the first Repair Café in Amsterdam in October 2009, where volunteer fixers mended visitors' broken items for free; thousands now run worldwide.
currencies.source_title: Repair Café (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: An old camcorder is exactly the kind of gadget that lands on a repair table.

currencies.name: Tool Lending
currencies.line: Hand and power tools lent out with a library card.
currencies.how: Bolts are earned by donating, sharpening or repairing tools for a lending library and spent on borrowing them. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The Berkeley Public Library opened its Tool Lending Library in 1979, letting residents borrow hand and power tools with a library card; it is among the oldest tool libraries still running.
currencies.source_title: Tool library (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Nobody needs to own a chainsaw for one weekend's job, which is the whole idea.

currencies.name: Talent Exchange
currencies.line: An online mutual-credit ledger linking local exchanges worldwide.
currencies.how: Members list offers and wants, earn Talents by providing goods or services and spend them with anyone on the network. Talents are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The Community Exchange System began in Cape Town in 2003 as the Cape Town Talent Exchange, an online interest-free mutual-credit ledger adapted from LETS; it now hosts exchanges in many countries.
currencies.source_title: A wealth of talents (Mail & Guardian)
currencies.noun_fit: The exchange lives online, and the heart on the laptop is for the community behind the ledger.

currencies.name: Sitter Scrip
currencies.tradition: Babysitting co-op scrip (Capitol Hill Babysitting Co-op)
currencies.line: Paper coupons for babysitting, and a famous lesson in scarcity.
currencies.how: Families earn Half-Hours by sitting for other members' children and spend them on sitting for their own, with enough issued to keep sitting flowing. Never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In the 1970s, families in the Capitol Hill Babysitting Co-op paid for childcare in scrip worth half an hour each; when too few coupons circulated, members hoarded them and sitting slumped.
currencies.source_title: Baby-Sitting the Economy (Slate, 1998)
currencies.noun_fit: Babysitters work the evening shift, when the bats come out.

currencies.name: Green Ledger
currencies.line: The first LETS: accounts start at zero, and nobody pays interest.
currencies.how: Members earn Leaves by offering goods or services, recorded as credits, and spend them on other members' offers; every account starts at zero. Leaves are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Michael Linton started the first LETS in Canada's Comox Valley in 1983, recording trades as 'green dollar' credits and debits on a central ledger, with no interest; the model spread worldwide.
currencies.source_title: Local exchange trading system (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: A whole planet captioned 'copy': the LETS model was copied by hundreds of groups around the world.

currencies.name: Heirloom Seed
currencies.line: Members mail each other heirloom seeds listed in a yearbook.
currencies.how: Envelopes are earned by saving and mailing heirloom seeds to members and spent on varieties others list. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Seed Savers Exchange was founded in 1975 after Diane Ott Whealy's grandfather gave her seeds his parents brought from Bavaria; members list saved varieties in a yearbook and swap them by mail.
currencies.source_title: Seed Savers Exchange (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Old film canisters are a gardener's favourite jar for saved seeds.

currencies.name: Weekend Farmhand
currencies.tradition: WWOOF (World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms)
currencies.line: Garden help swapped for a bed, meals and learning.
currencies.how: Rows are earned by helping in a member's home garden or smallholding and spent on a bed, a meal or lessons with another host; no money moves and no commercial farm takes part. Never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: In 1971 London secretary Sue Coppard organised the first 'Working Weekends on Organic Farms' in England; it became World Wide Opportunities on Organic Farms, linking hosts and volunteers without pay.
currencies.source_title: WWOOF (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Read the leafy head as garden weeds: weeding is the first job most farm volunteers learn.

currencies.name: Trade Exchange
currencies.line: Spare capacity swapped and booked in trade credits.
currencies.how: Neighbours earn Contras by lending spare capacity, such as a spare room, a trailer or an idle sewing machine, to other members and spend them on anyone's spare capacity. Never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Bartercard was founded on Australia's Gold Coast in 1991 as a business-to-business trade exchange where firms sell spare capacity for trade credits; tax authorities treat such trades as taxable.
currencies.source_title: Bartercard (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: A shop-counter classic, for an exchange built by businesses trading with businesses.

currencies.name: Released Book
currencies.line: Books labelled with an ID and released into the world.
currencies.how: Chapters are earned by registering and releasing a book for the next reader and spent on finding and logging books that others release. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Ron Hornbaker launched BookCrossing in Kansas City, Missouri, in April 2001: readers label a book with a unique ID and release it in a public place, and finders log it online to follow its journey.
currencies.source_title: BookCrossing (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: BookCrossers release books into the wild, like a whale set free.

currencies.name: Toy Loan
currencies.line: Toys borrowed and brought back, like library books.
currencies.how: Plays are earned by donating, cleaning or mending toys for a lending library and spent on borrowing toys and games. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: The first toy library is usually traced to Los Angeles in 1935, when a Depression-era program began lending toys; it continues as the county's Toy Loan Program. Sweden's Lekotek followed in 1963.
currencies.source_title: Toy library (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: A ball is the toy that gets borrowed most.

currencies.name: Camp Parcel
currencies.place: POW camps in Italy and Germany
currencies.tradition: Cigarette currency in WWII prisoner-of-war camps
currencies.line: Parcel goods traded in camp, priced by an agreed unit.
currencies.how: Rations are earned by contributing food, mending or skills in a closed community, such as a camp or expedition, and spent on goods others offer. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Economist R. A. Radford, himself a prisoner, described in 1945 how Allied POWs traded the contents of Red Cross parcels and priced goods in cigarettes, which became the camps' unit of account.
currencies.source_title: R. A. Radford, 'The Economic Organisation of a P.O.W. Camp', Economica (1945)
currencies.noun_fit: Camp prices rose and fell with parcel deliveries, a textbook chart in the making.

currencies.name: Esperanto Stay
currencies.line: Free beds and conversation for travellers who speak Esperanto.
currencies.how: Nights are earned by hosting travellers who speak a common language and spent on a stay with another host; conversation is the only fee. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Pasporta Servo began in 1966 as a list of Esperanto speakers willing to host fellow speakers for free; now run by TEJO, the World Esperanto Youth Organization, it has hosts in dozens of countries.
currencies.source_title: Pasporta Servo (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: A dictionary for a network held together by a shared constructed language.

currencies.name: Curbside Gift
currencies.line: Usable things given to neighbours instead of the landfill.
currencies.how: In a gift version, Gifts simply count items kept out of landfill: earned by passing on usable things and spent on requesting what neighbours offer. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Deron Beal started The Freecycle Network in Tucson, Arizona, in May 2003 as an email group for giving away usable items instead of landfilling them; it is a gift system with groups worldwide.
currencies.source_title: The Freecycle Network (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Hands reaching up for whatever a neighbour just offered: old things rising to a second life.

currencies.name: Cola for Vodka
currencies.line: Cola concentrate swapped for vodka when the ruble couldn't convert.
currencies.how: Crates are earned by supplying goods to a partner group in another place and spent on what that partner makes, with no cash crossing over. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Because the ruble was not convertible, a US cola maker agreed in 1972 to supply concentrate and bottling plants to the USSR in return for US rights to sell a Soviet vodka; a later deal added ships.
currencies.source_title: Pepsi (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: A soda can for the cola side of the Cold War's most famous swap.

currencies.name: Time Bank Hour
currencies.line: One hour of help earns one hour, whatever the task.
currencies.how: Hours are earned by helping another member, from childcare to tutoring, and spent on an hour of anyone's help; every hour counts the same. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Law professor Edgar S. Cahn developed Time Dollars in the early 1980s: members earn a credit for each hour spent helping someone and spend it on an hour of help. The model spread worldwide.
currencies.source_title: Time banking (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: An hour walking a neighbour's dog counts the same as an hour of tutoring.

currencies.name: Home Swap Club
currencies.line: Families trade homes for the holidays, with no rent either way.
currencies.how: Weeks are earned by lending your home, and sometimes your car, to a member family and spent on a stay in another member's home. They are never bought or cashed out.
currencies.fact: Organised home swapping dates to 1953, when European teachers founded Intervac so families could travel cheaply in summer; members stay in each other's homes, usually at the same time, rent-free.
currencies.source_title: Home exchange (Wikipedia)
currencies.noun_fit: Home swaps sometimes include the family car, so the taxi is part of the deal.
